summary: LunaHorizon is a free web app that shows the sky a lander will see at the Moon's south pole, before anyone goes. Pick a site and a date, and it counts the "Golden hours": when the Sun is up for power, Earth is in view, and a Deep Space Network dish can hear the lander, all at once. At the south pole the Sun slides along the horizon, so a single ridge can cut a lander's power and its link to Earth; a few hundred metres or a few days can decide whether a mission lasts 14 days or a few hours. LunaHorizon answers the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, where and when should we land, for CLPS mission planners, students and the public. It runs on NASA data plus JAXA partner data (NAIF SPICE, LRO LOLA terrain, SLDEM2015 with JAXA Kaguya, JPL Horizons and the Deep Space Network), and all 128 validation checks pass. The largest angle error is 0.000742°.
details:
Live app: https://lunahorizon.vercel.app

Full 4-minute film: https://youtu.be/9xmPoaiqwkE

Code and documentation: https://github.com/Mozahid-DIU/LunaHorizon

THE CHALLENGE

At the lunar south pole the Sun never climbs high. It slides along the horizon, so a single ridge can cut a lander's power and its link to Earth. A few hundred metres, or a few days, can decide whether a mission lasts 14 days or a few hours. LunaHorizon answers the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge: where, and when, should we land?

HOW IT WORKS

- A Python pipeline reads NASA SPICE kernels and finds the Sun's and Earth's positions over the Moon every hour for 2026–2030.

- It reads LRO LOLA elevation maps to build each site's real 360° skyline, out to 150 km.

- The browser turns these into the sky from any point and checks every 10 minutes for three things: the Sun above the skyline, Earth above it, and a DSN station (Goldstone, Madrid or Canberra) able to see the Moon. When all three hold at once, the hour is "Golden".

- No AI computes any number.

HOW WE KNOW IT IS RIGHT

- 128 of 128 checks pass against JPL Horizons, full SPICE and published terrain. The largest angle error is 0.000742°.

- On Chandrayaan-3, our predicted sunset fell on 4 Sep 2023, the same day ISRO put the lander to sleep.

WHAT IT DOES NOT DO (limits, stated openly)

- A skyline is only as fine as its terrain map: 20–240 m near the pole. Boulders and the lander's own shadow are not modelled.

- Comms is geometry only: antenna pointing, the link budget and DSN scheduling are not modelled.

- The power model is illustrative. It leaves out temperature, heaters, dust and charging losses.

- Every result is for one exact point. Ground nearby can differ, which is why the Landing Ellipse page exists.

Full list: docs/data.md, section 6.

FEATURES AND BENEFITS

- Explore: a south-pole map lit by the real Sun shows where Sun and Earth meet.

- Plan: the 360° sky from the lander's eye, hour by hour.

- Compare: two sites or dates side by side. The Shackleton rim gets 336 Golden hours and the IM-1 area gets 147.

- Best Dates: a search over 12 months for the best landing times.

- Landing Ellipse: within 500 m of the target, Golden hours range from 0 to 336.

- 3D Terrain: the real ground from LOLA heights, lit by the real Sun.

- Power: a simple battery model.

- Mission Replay: tests the engine on real landings.

- Classroom mode and plain-language explanations: teachers and students can use it with no training.

WHO BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- CLPS and other mission planners, for a quick first look.

- Students and teachers, through a real-data lesson on lunar light.

- The public, as an honest view of why the south pole is hard.

We want site choice at the south pole to be open and easy to check: anyone with a browser can see why one spot works and another fails, using the same NASA data mission teams use. The app is free, needs no install or account, and the code is open source (MIT).

WHAT WE'D BUILD NEXT

Finer terrain around new candidate sites; thermal and dust effects in the power model; relay-satellite coverage for the far side; exports for mission-design tools.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Data pipeline: Python 3.11, Skyfield, jplephem, NumPy, Pillow, requests, pytest

- Web app: Next.js and React (TypeScript), Three.js for 3D terrain, d3-scale for charts, hosted on Vercel

- Testing: Vitest (892 unit tests) and Playwright (461 browser tests)

- In-app helper: gpt-oss-120b (open-weight) through the Groq API

- Videos: FFmpeg, Playwright screen capture, Wan 2.2 on Kaggle (ComfyUI), Chatterbox TTS, faster-whisper

USE OF AI (where and how)

- Code: Claude Code (Anthropic) was our coding partner. Every design decision is ours, and every result is checked against independent references (128 checks, 1,350+ tests). Every prompt and how we verified it is logged in docs/ai-use.md.

- In-app text: gpt-oss-120b (via Groq) explains the engine's numbers in plain words. It never computes anything; an answer is shown only if every number in it matches our engine.

- Images and video: the lander and astronaut scenes in our videos are AI-generated (stills: ChatGPT; motion: Wan 2.2) and labelled in the videos as a simulation and as AI-generated. Every app shot is a real screen recording, and the Moon and Earth renders are made from NASA data.

- Audio: the radio voices are AI (Chatterbox), two cloned with permission from team members Khorshed Alam Mozahid and Jannatul Nur Tuli. The narration is the real voice of team member Navid Hasan. Subtitle timings come from faster-whisper.

- No NASA logos, flags or mission insignia appear in any AI-generated content.
